target: AG1’s claim that a national Election Day holiday would broadly remove scheduling barriers by giving people time off.
objection: Federal law does not require private employers to provide paid time off for a federal holiday, and many schedule-constrained low-income voters work in retail and service jobs for private employers, so a holiday would not reliably give them time off and could even impose lost-wage costs that deter voting.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday would meaningfully increase civic participation and turnout on its own.
objection: Research shows that an election holiday by itself is not an effective way to increase voter turnout compared with other voting-access reforms, so the holiday is unlikely to produce meaningful turnout gains on its own.

target: AG1’s reliance on a holiday as a better solution than other reforms.
objection: State laws requiring employers to give time off to vote and reforms such as automatic voter registration more directly and reliably address voting barriers than a federal holiday that does not guarantee paid leave.

target: AG2’s claim that the absence of a legal requirement for private employers to provide paid leave means an Election Day holiday would not relieve the scheduling barrier.
objection: Even without a guaranteed paid-leave mandate, federal holidays are widely observed in practice through school closures and many workplaces reducing operations or giving time off, so a holiday would still create usable non-working time and reduce the scheduling conflict for many voters.

target: AG2’s claim that the turnout objection defeats the holiday proposal because it is ineffective ‘by itself.’
objection: A holiday would do more than free up time; it would also frame voting as a celebrated civic act, which can increase civic motivation and engagement, so the holiday can still produce meaningful turnout gains even if it is not solely about logistics.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday would meaningfully help low-income workers and reliably protect their ability to vote.
objection: Because private employers are not required to provide paid time off, many low-income workers would still face lost wages or work schedules that conflict with voting, so the holiday would not reliably translate symbolic civic value into real voting time for them.

target: AG1’s broader claim that the holiday would improve turnout and access more reliably than alternatives.
objection: The research evidence still says an election holiday by itself is not an effective turnout strategy, while more direct reforms such as employer time-off rules and automatic voter registration are more reliable ways to improve access.

target: AG1’s claim that a federal Election Day holiday would reliably protect low-income workers’ time to vote.
objection: Low-income workers face acute economic and job-security pressures, and because private employers are not legally required to give paid holiday leave, a federal holiday would not reliably protect time for the most constrained voters; state-based employer-time-off rules and automatic voter registration are more dependable alternatives.

target: AG2’s claim that low-income workers would not have reliably protected time because private employers need not honor the holiday.
objection: The objection treats the holiday as depending only on private employer discretion, but federal holidays are widely observed in practice through school closures and many workplaces operating on reduced schedules, so the holiday would still reduce the time conflict that blocks many low-income and schedule-constrained voters.

target: AG1’s claim that school closures and reduced workplace schedules mean a holiday will reliably remove the key scheduling barrier for private-sector workers.
objection: Federal holiday status does not require private employers to close or guarantee time off, and many low-income workers in retail and service jobs would still be scheduled to work, so school closures and partial workplace reductions would not reliably eliminate the core time-conflict barrier for the most constrained voters.

target: AG2’s claim that a federal holiday would not reliably reduce scheduling barriers because not every private employer must comply.
objection: In practice, federal holidays are widely observed through school closures and many workplaces reducing schedules or closing partly, so designating Election Day as a holiday would still reduce time conflicts for a substantial share of voters, especially those constrained by school and normal work schedules.

target: AG2’s preference for state-based reforms over a holiday.
objection: A federal holiday would directly reduce the practical time-conflict barrier for many schedule-constrained voters while also signaling civic importance, so the policy is justified on its own terms rather than needing to be replaced by state-only reforms.
